title: Canary Upgrade Playbook — driver bindings & Terraform module notes (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic canary upgrade playbook focused on GPU driver / CUDA / NCCL change windows for Kubernetes node pools in private (VPC/on-prem) deployments. The goal is to provide a repeatable sequence of validation checks, Terraform module binding notes (inputs/outputs to watch), and incident-simulation tests so upgrades are low-risk and observable.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: SREs, platform engineers, and solutions engineers running private Redwood Private clusters (k8s + GPUs).
- Scope: single-region on-prem or VPC clusters with heterogeneous GPU nodes (A100/V100/RTX-class); Kubernetes versions between 1.24–1.28, driver versions 535.x–545.x, CUDA 11.8–12.3, NCCL 2.14–2.16.
- Not in scope: upstream OS package upgrades unrelated to driver stack, control plane upgrades (separate playbook).

Assumptions & prerequisites (must be satisfied before canary):
- Cluster backup/snapshots of critical state (etcd snapshot + kubeconfig safe copy).
- A target canary nodepool with 1–3 nodes that mirrors production node configuration (same GPU model, similar kernel, same container runtime).
- Terraform-managed nodepools; CI protects apply with manual approval gate.
- Monitoring: node exporter, nvidia-dcgm exporter, ccpm metrics, logging ingestion to central observability (Grafana + Loki).
- Rollback images are available: prior node-image + driver tarball, documented in A/B registry.

High-level upgrade sequence (single canary round):
1) Lock-change window and notify on-call / downstream teams.
2) Create canary node pool via Terraform (see Terraform notes below). Wait for nodes to become Ready.
3) Run preflight checks on canary nodes (hardware, kernel, existing driver info).
4) Drain a canary node, invoke driver upgrade (package or driver installer) via DaemonSet or node-image rollout.
5) Uncordon and run smoke validation (system checks + representative inference job).
6) Run stress and NCCL sanity tests, monitor metrics for 30–60 minutes.
7) If green, schedule a progressive rollout (batch sizes configurable). If failing, run rollback steps.

Preflight checks (commands & expected outputs):
- Verify node GPU visibility: `kubectl get nodes -o wide` then on node: `nvidia-smi -L` -> lists GPUs (3–8 lines depending on GPU count).
- Driver/CUDA baseline: `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version,cuda_version --format=csv` -> should match expected baseline for baseline pool.
- Kernel & modules: `uname -r` and `lsmod | grep nvidia` -> confirm driver module loaded.
- Container runtime integration: validate GPU devices exposed inside a test pod: `kubectl run gpu-test --image=nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:11.8-runtime --rm -it --restart=Never -- nvidia-smi` -> returns proper driver information.
- NVPeer/PCIe errors: `dmesg | grep -i nvrm` and `nvidia-smi errors` -> zero fatal errors expected.

Compatibility matrix (summary guidance — expand in lab notes):
- For A100 (Linux kernel >=5.4): recommended driver 535.x with CUDA 11.8 or driver 545.x with CUDA 12.1. NCCL 2.14 is compatible with CUDA 11.8; NCCL 2.16 with CUDA 12.x.
- For V100 (older kernels): prefer driver 470.x/510.x families with CUDA 11.4–11.7. If moving to CUDA 12, ensure kernel >=5.10 and validate with NCCL 2.16.
- RTX-class (consumer): driver buckets may vary—use conservative driver pinning and validate PCIe power settings.

Notes: this matrix is intentionally brief. Before any broad rollout, expand to a table in Confluence listing exact kernel, driver, CUDA, NCCL combinations validated in lab.

Terraform module notes (practical items to include in module & CI):
- Inputs to expose: `gpu_driver_version` (string), `node_image_tag` (string), `node_taints` (list), `max_unavailable` (int), `canary_size` (int), `node_labels` (map).
- Outputs to export: `canary_nodepool_id`, `driver_artifact_sha`, `node_image_digest` -> used by downstream approvals.
- Guardrails: add plan-time checks via CI that validate `gpu_driver_version` is within allowed set (policy file or lookup in a shared allowed-versions artifact). Fail plan if unapproved.
- Drift detection: run a terraform plan every 24 hours in CI against prod nodepools to detect unexpected driver or image changes. Report via ticket bot.
- Blue/Green vs in-place: prefer creating a separate node-image (blue) + nodepool and migrating pods; in-place driver installs are only for emergency-and-tested scenarios.
- Module example (pseudo-snippet to include in module README):
  - `module "gpu_nodes" { source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//modules/gpu-node" gpu_driver_version = var.gpu_driver_version node_image_tag = var.node_image_tag canary_size = 2 }`

Canary validation checklist (detailed):
- Cluster health: `kubectl get cs` and `kubectl get nodes` all Ready.\- Node-level: `nvidia-smi` shows driver version = target, GPU memory accessible, no ECC errors.\- Pod-level: deploy 2 representative inference pods (one short-latency chat call, one embedding batch) with same resource requests and run 100 requests each. Record 95th/99th percentiles. Latency regression threshold: +20% at 95th or any error spike -> fail.\- NCCL multi-GPU test: run `nccl-tests` (all_reduce, all_gather) across 2–4 GPUs in the canary node; expect 0 errors and throughput within +/-10% of baseline.\- DCGM exporter coverage: verify metrics for GPU_utilization, ecc_errors, power_draw; set short-term alert if any new error counter increments.\- Logs: check dmesg for new nvrm errors; check kubelet logs for device plugin warnings.

Observability and SLOs to watch during the canary window:
- Token per-second throughput and per-route 95th latency (observability tags to include `nodepool:canary-gpu-v1`).\- GPU error counters (ECC, volatile memory errors).\- Pod evictions and OOM kills.\- NCCL socket/timeouts.

Stress & incident simulation tests (run after smoke is green):
- Load spike: send a 3x burst to inference pods for 5 min; watch queueing, GPU memory saturation, and time-to-first-byte.\- Network partition simulation: isolate canary nodes from internal registry for 2 minutes (simulate image pull timeouts) and observe node re-registration.
- Driver failure simulation: on one canary node, unload driver module and re-load (modprobe -r nvidia; modprobe nvidia) and observe kubelet and container restarts. Document exact outcomes.

Rollback steps (fast path):
1) If driver-level fatal errors or degraded node behavior, cordon node(s) and scale up prior-healthy nodepool created with previous node-image.
2) If a node is unhealthy post-driver rollback, escalate to hardware engineer to rule out ephemeral HW/firmware regressions.
3) Re-run automated post-rollback smoke and stress tests to confirm restored telemetry.

Postmortem data collection (if failure):
- Collect: `kubectl get pods -A -o wide`, node `dmesg`, `journalctl -u kubelet`, `nvidia-smi -q`, `kubectl describe node <node>`, DCGM exporter snapshots (JSON), terraform state delta from CI.\- Create an incident ticket and attach these artifacts to the canary-run record.

Open questions / TODOs (items to resolve before broad rollout):
- Constrain allowed driver families via centralized artifact (who owns this list?).
- Define exact latency regression gates per customer tier (S1/S2).
- Add sentinel-like policies in Terraform Cloud to reject risky driver versions.
- Expand compatibility matrix to include node-image OS patch level vs driver.

Appendix: quick command cheatsheet:
- `kubectl get nodes -L beta.kubernetes.io/os -o wide`
- `ssh core@<node> sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version,cuda_version --format=csv`
- `kubectl run -it --rm gpu-smoke --image=nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:11.8-runtime --restart=Never -- nvidia-smi`
- `kubectl logs -n kube-system nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset-<pod>`
- `nccl-tests/build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 512M -f 2 -g 2`

Reviewer notes:
- This is intentionally prescriptive but not final. I propose we run two canary rounds (different driver family and node-image) in staging this sprint, capture telemetry and update the matrix.

If you take action: please add test results to the Confluence compatibility page linked above and update the `allowed-drivers.json` artifact in the terraform-modules repo.

Author: Asha Patel (eng-private-deployments)
